title: MILITARY PRESSURES AGAINST NVN: JULY - OCTOBER, 1964
summary:
Declassified per Exec utive Order 13526, Sectio n 3.3 NND Project Number: NND 633 16 . By: NWD Date: 2011
TOP SECRET - Sensitive
MILITARY PRESSURES AGAINST NVN: JULY - OCTOBER, 1964

title: SUMMARY and ANALYSIS
summary: Declassified 1964 analysis of U.S. pressures against North Vietnam. Covers disillusion over South Vietnam's deteriorating politics under Khanh, and the emerging consensus for graduated pressure on Hanoi, deferred for tactical reasons (elections, GVN instability, Laos). Details the August 1964 Tonkin Gulf incidents, U.S. reprisals, and the Congressional resolution, and their effects on resolve and flexibility. Discusses Rostow's thesis on striking insurgent sources and its critique. Describes the September 7 principals' meeting, JCS and McNamara proposals, NSAM 314 limited measures, and the table of contents with appendices.

title: MILITARY PRESSURES AGAINST NV~, JULY - OCTOBER 1964
summary: Declassified chronology of U.S. military pressures against North Vietnam, July–October 1964. Covers resumed DESOTO destroyer patrols after a DRV PT-boat attack on USS Maddox, covert GVN raids, U.S. reprisal strikes, Congressional briefings and the Tonkin Gulf Resolution, and Khanh's rise and fall. Also covers Laotian diplomacy (three princes' meeting, U Thant's conference call), internal memos on escalation (Bundy, CJCS, McNaughton, Rostow thesis, Taylor, State), NSAM 314, the third Tonkin Gulf incident, and approval of covert cross-border and Laotian air operations.

title: PROLOGUE: ACTIONS AND PROGRAMS UNDERWAY
summary: Covers pressures applied against North Vietnam by July 1964: U.S. armed reconnaissance over Laos with Souvanna Phouma's approval, T-28 support for a Royal Laotian counteroffensive near Muong Soui, and public signals of U.S. commitment (Thailand stockpiles, Da Nang air base, Air Force Day display). It also describes Blair Seaborn's warnings to Hanoi, a domestic public-information campaign (Robert Manning as coordinator, NSAM, public pamphlet), covert operations including DE SOTO patrols (Craig, Maddox), South Vietnamese coastal junk patrols, and OPLAN 34A raids. Planned cross-border operations in Laos and proposals (a Congressional Resolution, UN case, force deployments, graduated military force) were left on the shelf without clear decisions.

title: THE TO~KIN GULF CRISIS
key_items: 1. To c ontinue the patrols in the Gulf of Tonkin off the coast of North Viet nam .
summary: A declassified account of the 1964 Gulf of Tonkin crisis. It describes the first incident (August 2, 1964), in which North Vietnamese PT boats attacked the USS Maddox after South Vietnamese raids on coastal islands, and the U.S. protest and augmented patrols that followed. It then covers the second incident (August 4), a disputed night attack on the Maddox and C. Turner Joy, and the Washington response: reprisal air strikes, Congressional consultations, deployments to the Western Pacific, and the Tonkin Gulf Resolution. The text assesses the attacks as likely genuine, possibly unplanned, and notes the Administration's exploitation of them for political and strategic ends, including deterrence messages to Hanoi and the UN.

title: POST-TONKIN POLICY ASSESSMENTS

nodes.title: DILEMMAS IN hAOS
nodes.summary: Describes post-Tonkin Gulf U.S. policy assessments: the incidents' impact on policymakers, who learned the U.S. had fewer options. Covers Laos dilemmas: the Polish six-nation preliminary conference proposal, Soviet threats to withdraw as co-chairman, French and Chinese push for a Geneva-type 14-nation conference, British efforts, Laotian military gains at Operation Triangle, and the 'don't rock the boat' policy against bombing Panhandle infiltration routes.

nodes.title: CONCERN OVER PRESSURES FOR NEGOrrIATIONS
nodes.summary: Describes the Administration's concern over Geneva conference pressures after the Tonkin Gulf incidents, including UN Secretary General U Thant's call to reconvene the 14-Nation assembly, the French call for a pacification conference for Indochina, a Chinese editorial favoring a Geneva settlement, and North Vietnam's insistence on Geneva. It covers a State Department proposal to drop the demand for Pathet Lao withdrawal from the Plaine des Jarres, the unfavorable reactions (including Ambassador Taylor's cable warning of demoralization and lost resolve), and the view that a conference would be disadvantageous.

nodes.title: CONCERN OVER TOEKIN REPRISAL SIGNALS
nodes.summary: Analysis of Administration reactions to the Tonkin Gulf reprisals. Officials saw them as the strongest U.S. resolve expression to date, boosting South Vietnamese morale and interrupting communist momentum, but doubted lasting effect. Ambassador Taylor called it an isolated incident not yet addressing DRV subversion. Bundy, CINCPAC, and JCS urged sustained military pressure, cross-border air and ground operations into Laos, and readiness buildup. Officials agreed further escalation was needed, with no estimate of duration or scope.

nodes.title: RRASSERT ICN OF THE ROSTOW THESIS
nodes.summary: Describes Walt Rostow's thesis, circulated after the Tonkin Gulf incidents and first presented to President Johnson in December 1963, that insurgencies backed by external powers must be countered by neutralizing that support. Covers his 1964 formulation of limited, graduated military and political-economic pressure to change a state's cost-benefit calculation, the four factors affecting that calculation, coercive measures such as blockade and targeted strikes, and the view that morale and bargaining gains are secondary. Notes OSD/ISA's later analysis.

nodes.title: ACCOMPANYING PAUSE IN PRESSURES
nodes.summary: Describes a 1964 declassified account of the 'holding phase' after the Tonkin Gulf incident: the US paused provocative actions, but relaxed rules of engagement (15 Aug 1964) allowing attacks and hot pursuit, and advanced planning for GVN-US cross-border ground operations (MACV, Westmoreland noted US control could be marginal). It covers South Vietnam's political instability (Taylor's pessimism, Khanh's self-proclaimed presidency and Vung Tau Charter, August protests, Khanh's resignation and return), perceived increases in communist infiltration with uncertain evidence, and Washington's growing sense that some action was urgently needed.

summary: Post-Tonkin Gulf U.S. policy assessments: officials learned U.S. options were fewer. Laos dilemmas include Polish six-nation proposal, Soviet co-chair withdrawal threats, French/Chinese push for a 14-nation Geneva-type conference, British efforts, Laotian gains at Operation Triangle, and a 'don't rock the boat' stance against bombing Panhandle routes. Administration feared Geneva pressures (U Thant, French, Chinese, North Vietnamese), considered dropping the Plaine des Jarres withdrawal demand, and opposed a conference. Reprisals seen as resolve signals but of limited lasting effect; advisers urged sustained pressure and cross-border operations. Rostow's thesis on neutralizing external support via graduated pressure is outlined. A 1964 holding phase paused provocations while loosening rules of engagement and planning cross-border operations amid South Vietnamese political instability and infiltration concerns.

title: NEXT COURSES OF ACT ION

nodes.title: STRATEGY MEETING IN SEPTEMBER
nodes.summary: Covers early September 1964 US deliberations on pressuring North Vietnam: a 7 September Washington strategy meeting (Johnson, Rusk, McNamara, Wheeler, Taylor, McCone) weighing JCS proposals for provocative and sustained bombing, which were rejected as premature given weak GVN. Principals instead recommended resuming Gulf of Tonkin DE SOTO patrols, 34A maritime operations, limited Laos corridor operations, and tit-for-tat responses. Approved by 10 September NSAM, which excluded air strikes under 34A for now.

nodes.title: Naval Operations
nodes.summary: Describes the 1964 Tonkin Gulf naval incidents: the destroyers USS Morton and USS Edwards on DESOTO patrol (12 Sept) detected radar contacts at night on the 18th, fired after a warning shot, and reported hits with no return fire. Ammunition counts are given. President Johnson suspended DESOTO patrols until February 1965. Covert GVN maritime operations resumed in October under tight approval by OSD, State, and the White House, including probes, a junk capture attempt, bombardment of radar sites, and underwater demolition raids on coastal bridges.

nodes.title: Actions in Laos
nodes.summary: Covers U.S. planning for covert cross-border operations in Laos's Panhandle after NSAM 314 (Sept.–Oct.): Saigon mission talks on air strikes (military vs. psychological aims), recommended RLAF T-28 strikes with U.S. support, ground operations in three areas (only Route 9 penetrations approved in principle), JCS proposals, the 6 October authorization, and the decision to defer Route 7 strikes. Also covers the 13 October U.S. CAP approval, later-authorized U.S. strikes, and no cross-border ground authorization. Discusses Laotian tripartite talks in Paris, the failed cease-fire, Ambassador Unger and Taylor's views, State Department negotiating tactics, and GVN morale as the key constraint. Ends with concerns about South Vietnam's stability as a base for wider action.

nodes.title: General Scheme
nodes.summary: The text covers US planning for overt military operations against North Vietnam, planned to begin around January 1965. It discusses NSAM 288 contingency OPLAN 37-64 with graduated air strikes, Ambassador Taylor's 1 January 1965 target D-Day and readiness goals, and the August State Department strategy and NSAM 314 limited pressures through December. It also covers OSD/ISA proposals: infiltration-route strikes, then POL, Haiphong mining, bridges and railroads, plus McNaughton's September plan and escalating GVN-US actions. Finally, it notes the September conference hopes for GVN strength and public justification of maritime operations.

nodes.title: Reservations
Reservations (intro)
nodes.summary: By October 1961, top presidential advisers believed North Vietnam would eventually need overt military pressure to resolve DRV-sponsored insurgency in South Vietnam and Laos; earlier views had been conditional and now reflected inevitability. A 1964 OSD/ISA critique (with State Policy Planning Council input) of the Rostow thesis, that covert aggression justifies attacks on its source, identified three conditions for success: limited actions with total commitment, national consensus, and vital U.S. interests at stake (only Laos-Vietnam arguably qualified). Further conditions included publicly proving external support, exposing intelligence, identifying targets, communicating limited objectives, and verifying compliance. The critique warned of domestic and international opposition, advised against declaratory adoption without readiness to act, and urged serious examination of escalation risks. Agencies differed on five issues: acknowledging GVN maritime operations, tit-for-tat reprisals, handling enemy reactions, GVN/U.S. readiness, and links between pressure and negotiations.

nodes.title: JCS vie';.Ts
nodes.summary: Declassified JCS and senior military deliberations (1964-65 period) on Southeast Asia: officials disagreed on officially acknowledging GVN maritime operations (CINCPAC, Wheeler, service chiefs) and on deliberately provoking DRV actions, though all supported reprisals greater in degree than provocations. Debate covered preparing for enemy reactions, including Westmoreland's request for U.S. ground forces to secure bases versus JCS refusal to precommit forces under OPLAN 37-64, and an Air Force proposal to rely more on tactical air. Chiefs agreed on increasing pressure on North Vietnam via air power, opposed B-57 VNAF training, and showed little interest in negotiations.

Section 'Reservations': By October 1961, presidential advisers saw overt military pressure on North Vietnam as eventually necessary against DRV-backed insurgency in South Vietnam and Laos. A 1964 OSD/ISA critique of the Rostow thesis (covert aggression justifies attacks on its source) lists conditions for success: limited actions with total commitment, national consensus, vital interests at stake (only Laos-Vietnam arguably qualifies), public proof of external support, intelligence exposure, target identification, communicated limited objectives, and verification. It warns of domestic and international opposition and escalation risks, and disagreements over acknowledging GVN maritime operations, reprisals, enemy reactions, readiness, and links to negotiations. JCS deliberations (1964-65) split on acknowledging maritime operations and provoking DRV actions, favored air pressure, and showed little interest in negotiations.

nodes.title: Saigon Embassy views
nodes.summary: Saigon Embassy views under Ambassador Taylor: he opposed his military colleagues on several issues, including leaking GVN maritime operations, tit-for-tat bombing, and major U.S. ground commitment. He saw enemy ground assaults as the greater base threat and backed U.S. base-security deployments, partly to keep ARVN free for combat. He favored B-57 training for the VNAF, avoided negotiations until North Vietnam faced more pressure, and after Khanh's political upheaval opposed overt action against the DRV, urging first GVN strengthening.

nodes.title: OSD views
nodes.summary: OSD (Office of the Secretary of Defense) views on Vietnam policy: consistent support for surfacing GVN maritime operations; regarded negotiations as necessary to end the insurgency, with pressure on the DRV to improve U.S. bargaining position. OSD was cautious about overt attacks on North Vietnam, worried about readiness (POL and ordnance stocks), and its 'Plan of Action' minimized risk. Views on tit-for-tat reprisals were unclear, and prudence dominated preparations for enemy reactions, including countering a Chinese intervention without large U.S. ground forces. OSD also questioned a USAF ground force reduction study and backed JCS disapproval of an MACV troop request.

nodes.title: State views
nodes.summary: State Department views on Vietnam policy in 1964, channeled via the Secretary of State and Assistant Secretary for Far Eastern Affairs. Administration mostly followed State's advice: support for strengthening the GVN and non-overt pressure, though B-57 training for the VNAF was overruled on JCS advice and maritime acknowledgment failed due to GVN objections. State favored reprisals matched to VC acts in principle but not always, saw escalation as useful for GVN morale without provoking it yet, and accepted future deliberate provocations. It viewed an international conference as inevitable but only after hurting North Vietnam and convincing South Vietnam of U.S. resolve. Rusk, Bundy, and Rostow avoided committing U.S. ground forces.

nodes.title: CIA views
nodes.summary: Declassified 1964 CIA analysis on Vietnam: CIA views lack policy recommendations but assess enemy reactions. Intelligence expected limited communist responses to maritime ops and tit-for-tat strikes (defensive measures, propaganda, Chinese logistics). Heavier sustained reprisals might prompt DRV diplomatic moves and VC restraint. Air attacks might prompt a large DRV force deployment, though Hanoi would likely choose a conservative course; China intervenes only if the mainland is struck or ground forces occupy DRV/Laos areas. Communists sought a neutralist coalition soon. GVN political decay was predicted. Ends with a draft Southeast Asia resolution citing the Geneva Accords.

summary: Section 'Next Courses of Action' covers 1964 US Vietnam deliberations: the 7 September strategy meeting rejecting premature bombing, resuming Tonkin patrols and covert 34A operations (NSAM approved 10 Sept), Tonkin Gulf naval incidents and DESOTO suspension, covert Laos cross-border operations under NSAM 314, planned overt action against North Vietnam (~Jan 1965), and agency views: JCS favoring air pressure, Taylor opposing tit-for-tat and ground commitment, OSD cautious on readiness, State favoring non-overt pressure, and CIA predicting limited communist reactions, with China intervening only if mainland struck.

title: TOP SECRET

nodes.title: TOP SECRET (intro)
nodes.summary: A 1964 TOP SECRET draft Southeast Asia resolution, declassified in 2011, responds to alleged North Vietnamese and Chinese Communist aggression against South Vietnam and Laos, citing violations of the 1954 Geneva Accords and 1962 Laos agreements. It states U.S. non-territorial aims, pledges armed and economic assistance to South Vietnam and Laos at presidential discretion, and authorizes funds for fiscal years 1964 and 1965, with blanks for amounts, plus personnel and allowance provisions. The document also includes a Senate committee letter (Fulbright) requesting Tonkin Gulf incident information and a Secretary McNamara statement, and the committee chairman asks that testimony not be released publicly yet.

nodes.title: RELEc\SIXG OF DOCU:,\IEXTS
nodes.summary: Transcript of a congressional executive session on whether a Cabinet officer's (Secretary McNamara's) prepared statement may be released. Senator Morse argues the committee should not restrict the Secretary or the administration witness under separation-of-powers doctrine. The Chairman proposes simultaneous release of the staff report and Secretary's statement; Senator Gore asks to defer judgment until the statement is read. Senator Hickenlooper says release responsibility lies with the committee and urges comity. Senator Lausche condemns leaks of closed-session material to newspapers and calls for an investigation. Senator Morse clarifies his position, and Senator Lausche disputes a witness's claim about missiles fired at U.S. ships.

nodes.title: STAFF STUDY m::F1::SELl
nodes.summary: Excerpt of a 1964 Senate hearing transcript on the Tonkin Gulf incident. The Secretary of Defense (McNamara) and Chairman discuss a withheld staff study, which the Secretary says was denied to the Secretary and whose author lacked full access to information. The text covers an addendum with unnamed contacts claiming no missiles were fired, and Senator Lausche and others' questions. It then argues the attacks on the USS Maddox and Turner Joy on August 2 and 4 were real, unprovoked by South Vietnamese naval operations (OPLAN 34A), and that U.S. destroyers had no connection to those raids.

nodes.title: REnEW OF F,-\CTS OF ATTACK
REnEW OF F,-\CTS OF ATTACK (intro)
nodes.summary: The text is a 1964 official account of the Gulf of Tonkin incidents. It covers the unprovoked August 2 attack on the USS Maddox in international waters by North Vietnamese torpedo boats, and the Maddox's defense. It describes the U.S. protest note, the August 4 reports of a second attack, the consultations and the decision to order an air strike. It rebuts claims that the De Soto patrol was illegitimate or provocative, asserts the 3-mile territorial limit, and denies any link to South Vietnamese raids. It also addresses doubts about whether a second attack occurred and details the ships' engagement on the night of August 4.

nodes.title: RJ~porii-soF EYE,YITXESSES
RJ~porii-soF EYE,YITXESSES (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes eyewitness sightings from USS Turner Joy and USS Maddox of a torpedo wake passing abeam, gunfire and hits on a target that vanished from radar with black smoke, a searchlight sweeping toward Turner Joy and extinguished when aircraft approached, and silhouettes of attacking P-4 boats seen by four Turner Joy crewmen who accurately sketched them. Also covers Maddox crew and Marine machine gunners seeing lights and a boat, and Attack Squadron 52 pilots from Ticonderoga sighting a wake and anti-aircraft bursts near the destroyers.

nodes.title: INTELLIGEXCE HEPOItTS
nodes.summary: Declassified account of the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incidents. Intelligence reports claimed North Vietnam prepared torpedo boat attacks on US destroyers, and that an engagement on August 4 occurred with North Vietnamese ships lost. Defense Department review concluded a deliberate attack occurred on the Maddox and Turner Joy on August 4, endorsed by Vice Adm. Johnson, Adm. Moorer, and Lt. Gen. Burchinal. The text says the persistent doubts stem from confusing August 4 with a September 18 incident, which had no credible evidence of attack. Later captured North Vietnamese naval personnel gave accounts; one denied PT boat involvement, contradicted by another officer identifying a PT squadron commander as participating.

nodes.title: SCI'FICIEXT E\-WE X CE ,\,.ATL_\uLE TO SUPPOIlT COXCLlJSIOX
nodes.summary: Excerpt from a Gulf of Tonkin (August 1964) congressional testimony by the Secretary of Defense. It covers doubts about whether a second attack occurred, given fragmentary and delayed reports (radar contacts, torpedo sightings, searchlights, gunfire, claimed sinkings, a task group commander's certainty), and the President's order issued before full information arrived. It argues the August 2 attack was repulsed, the protest warned of consequences, the patrol was ordered to stay 11 miles offshore, and a conspiracy to fabricate the incident would be implausible. The chairman then opens questions.

nodes.title: !XTEJ:XAT, T}WUBL'ES OF KIL\Xn GO\,EnX~IEXT
nodes.summary: Declassified 1964-era congressional hearing excerpt on the Khanh government in South Vietnam, which overthrew the Minh junta in January 1964. It covers reported serious trouble and dissension within the government in spring and early summer 1964, followed by a series of changes among its members. Chairman questions Secretary McNamara about a recent remark that South Vietnam was on the verge of defeat three and a half years earlier. McNamara concedes he misstated the date, saying he meant two and a half years earlier (July 1961), and says he would need the full transcript to verify.

Eyewitness accounts from USS Turner Joy and USS Maddox of torpedo wakes, gunfire, a vanished radar target, a searchlight, and P-4 boat silhouettes, plus Maddox and Marine sightings and Ticonderoga pilot reports of a wake and anti-aircraft fire. Declassified reports on the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incidents claim a deliberate August 4 attack, with doubts attributed to confusion with a September 18 incident; captured North Vietnamese accounts conflict on PT boat involvement. Secretary of Defense testimony addresses fragmentary reports, the August 2 attack, patrol orders, and the implausibility of fabrication. Hearing excerpt on the Khanh government in South Vietnam covers 1964 dissension and cabinet changes, and McNamara's misstated date for the country's near-defeat (corrected to July 1961).

Official 1964 account of the Gulf of Tonkin incidents: the unprovoked August 2 torpedo-boat attack on USS Maddox and its defense, the U.S. protest, the disputed August 4 second attack and ensuing engagement, the air-strike decision, and rebuttals on the De Soto patrol's legitimacy, the 3-mile limit, and any link to South Vietnamese raids. Eyewitness and pilot reports (torpedo wakes, gunfire, vanished radar target, searchlight, boat silhouettes) and declassified and captured accounts conflict on whether a second attack occurred. Also covers Defense Secretary testimony, and a hearing on South Vietnam's Khanh government and McNamara's misdated near-defeat (corrected to July 1961).

summary: A declassified 1964 TOP SECRET draft Southeast Asia resolution responds to alleged North Vietnamese and Chinese aggression, cites the Geneva Accords, pledges aid to South Vietnam and Laos, and authorizes FY1964-65 funds. It includes a Fulbright committee request for Tonkin Gulf information and debate over releasing McNamara's statement. It also covers a withheld staff study, the disputed August 2 and 4 attacks on USS Maddox and Turner Joy, conflicting eyewitness reports, and a hearing on South Vietnam's Khanh government.

title: SOUTHFJ\..ST ASIA HESOLUTImr 3::./
summary: The Tonkin Gulf Resolution (Public Law 88-408, approved August 10, 1964). Congress approves presidential action to repel armed attacks on US forces and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia, citing North Vietnamese attacks on US naval vessels in international waters. It declares southeast Asian peace vital to US interests and pledges to assist treaty members (SEATO) with force if requested. The resolution expires when the President determines peace is assured by UN or other action, or earlier by concurrent resolution.

summary: Footnotes (numbered 1–155) from a declassified U.S. government history of Vietnam-era decisions, mostly citing 1964 sources. Topics include: U.S. Navy reconnaissance aircraft shot down over Laos and armed escort flights; Honolulu Conference and pressures against North Vietnam; Gulf of Tonkin incidents (Aug 2 and 4, 1964) and congressional resolution debate; rules of engagement and cross-border operations; Rostow thesis analysis; NSAM 308, 314; SNIE estimates; and Saigon/Vientiane embassy cables, memoranda, and interviews. Sources are classified memos, cables, press accounts, and testimony.
